source: FAO/OIE/World Bank, "Good Practices for Biosecurity in the Pig Sector - Issues and Options in Developing and Transition Countries", FAO Animal Production and Health Paper No. 169, Rome, 2010.
text: For small-scale confined pig production (pigs kept in a pen rather than roaming), confinement makes several extra protective measures possible on top of the scavenging-system basics: fence the pig area and control who and what enters, including birds, rodents, cats and dogs where feasible; keep newly purchased pigs in a separate quarantine pen for a minimum of 30 days before mixing them with the existing herd; group pigs by age/production stage rather than mixing ages in the same pen; provide visitors with clean footwear/clothing for use only on the farm, and have people wash their hands on entry; assign equipment (buckets, tools) to this farm only rather than sharing it with neighboring pig farms; remove manure from pens daily rather than letting it accumulate; and thoroughly clean and, where possible, disinfect a pen after a group of pigs leaves it and before the next group arrives.
